title: Hail Damage Insurance Claim in Texas: A Step-by-Step Guide
seo_title: Hail Damage Insurance Claim Texas: Step-by-Step Guide
meta_description: Filing a hail damage insurance claim in Texas? What to do after the storm, how to check your roof safely, document damage and avoid scams.
body_html:
Hail is a fact of life across much of Texas, and a single storm can leave dents, cracked shingles, and broken windows across an entire neighborhood. What you do in the days after matters: a calm, well-documented claim tends to go far more smoothly than a rushed one. This guide walks you through it, from the first look outside to the final payment.

This is general information, not insurance or legal advice. Texas policies vary widely, so read your own policy and ask your insurer, a licensed public adjuster, or an attorney about your specific situation.

Right after the storm: safety first

  • Wait until the storm has fully passed. Hail often comes with lightning, high winds, and sometimes tornadoes.
  • Watch for hazards: downed power lines, broken glass, and hanging limbs. Treat any downed line as live and report it to your utility.
  • Stay off the roof. Wet or damaged shingles are slippery, and falls are a real risk. Let a professional handle anything that requires climbing.
  • Protect the inside if water is coming in: move belongings, set out buckets, and run towels or a wet/dry vacuum.

If the storm knocked out your power, keep flashlights handy and avoid candles near damaged areas or anything wet.

How to check for hail damage from the ground

You can learn a lot without a ladder. Walk the property slowly and look for:

  • Soft metals: dents in gutters, downspouts, roof vents, AC condenser fins, mailboxes, and window wraps. These are often the easiest signs to spot and photograph.
  • Granules from asphalt shingles collecting at the bottom of downspouts or in gutters.
  • Visible shingle damage through binoculars or a phone camera zoom: dark spots, cracks, missing pieces, or exposed mat.
  • Siding and trim: cracks, holes, or chipped paint on the side facing the storm.
  • Windows and screens: cracked panes and torn or dented screens.
  • Fences, decks, patio furniture, and outdoor lights.
  • Interior clues: new ceiling stains or drips, especially in the attic after rain.

Hail damage on a roof is not always obvious from below. If you see dented gutters or vents, it is reasonable to have the roof inspected by a reputable roofer or to wait for your insurer's adjuster.

Document everything before cleanup

  1. Photograph the hail itself if you can, with a coin or ruler for scale, and note the date and time.
  2. Take wide shots of each side of the house, then close-ups of every dent, crack, or hole.
  3. Record a narrated video walking around the property.
  4. Save local weather reports or news coverage showing hail in your area on that date.
  5. Photograph interior water damage and damaged belongings. A home inventory for insurance makes the contents part much easier.
  6. Keep receipts for tarps, emergency repairs, and any temporary lodging.

Prevent further damage

Most policies require you to take reasonable steps to protect your property after a loss. That might mean tarping a damaged roof section (by a professional), boarding a broken window, or drying out wet areas. Reasonable emergency repair costs are often reimbursable, so keep receipts. Hold off on permanent repairs, like a full roof replacement, until your insurer has inspected or agreed in writing. If water got inside, our water damage insurance claim tips cover drying and documentation.

Filing your claim promptly

  1. Pull out your policy and declarations page. Look for your wind and hail deductible, roof coverage terms, and any cosmetic damage exclusions.
  2. Report the claim soon after the storm. Check your policy for notice and proof-of-loss deadlines. Waiting can make it harder to connect damage to a specific storm.
  3. Get a claim number and your adjuster's name and contact details.
  4. Be there for the inspection if you can. Point out everything you found, including soft metal dents, interior stains, and outbuildings.
  5. Get an independent estimate from a qualified contractor so you can compare it with the insurer's.
  6. Keep a claim log of every call, email, and visit, with dates and names.
  7. Ask for written explanations of any denial or partial payment, including the policy language relied on.

Texas-specific things to know

Wind and hail deductibles

Many Texas homeowners policies use a separate wind and hail deductible, often set as a percentage of your dwelling coverage rather than a flat dollar amount. A percentage deductible can be much larger than people expect, so do the math before the next storm season.

Roof coverage terms

Some Texas policies pay roof claims on an actual cash value basis, apply a roof payment schedule based on age, or exclude purely cosmetic hail damage (like dents in metal roofing that do not affect function). Check your policy for these provisions; they can change your payout significantly.

Coastal windstorm coverage

In designated coastal areas, wind and hail coverage may come from the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association (TWIA) instead of your homeowners policy, which means a separate policy and separate claim process.

Deductibles and contractors

Texas law prohibits contractors from offering to waive, absorb, or rebate your insurance deductible. Be cautious of anyone who promises a "free roof." You are responsible for paying your deductible.

Where to get help

The Texas Department of Insurance publishes consumer guidance on storm claims, can answer questions, and accepts complaints about insurers and adjusters. Weather risk also varies a lot across the state; our Texas climate regions guide explains why.

Roofers and storm chasers: how to protect yourself

After big hailstorms, out-of-town crews often go door to door. Many are legitimate, but some leave homeowners with poor work and no one to call. Texas does not have a statewide license for residential roofers, so your own vetting matters.

  • Prefer established local contractors with a physical address and references you can call.
  • Ask for proof of insurance, including liability and workers' compensation.
  • Get written estimates from more than one contractor.
  • Read before you sign. Be careful with contracts that give a contractor control of your claim or assign your insurance benefits to them.
  • Avoid large upfront payments. Pay as work is completed, and keep records of every payment.
  • Be wary of pressure: "today only" pricing, claims of a free roof, or a contractor offering to negotiate your claim. Texas law generally bars contractors from acting as public adjusters; a licensed public adjuster or an attorney can represent you on a claim.

If the payment seems too low

  • Compare the insurer's estimate line by line with your contractor's.
  • Ask for a re-inspection and send additional photos or evidence.
  • Review whether your policy's appraisal clause applies. See our insurance appraisal tips.
  • Consider a licensed public adjuster. Read how public adjusters help with insurance claims.

Frequently asked questions

Can I file a hail claim if I did not notice damage right away?

Possibly, but delays can make it harder to tie damage to a specific storm. Check your policy for notice deadlines and report as soon as you find damage.

Will filing a hail claim raise my premium?

It can depend on your insurer and claims history. Ask your agent or insurer how claims may affect your policy before you decide.

Do renters need to file a hail claim?

The landlord's policy usually covers the building. Renters may need their own renters insurance claim for damaged belongings or a car claim for a dented vehicle. See our guide to renters storm damage claims.

Does homeowners insurance cover hail damage to my car?

Generally no. Hail damage to a vehicle is typically handled under the comprehensive coverage of an auto policy.

Texas hail season brings a lot of shared experience. If you are mid-claim or just went through one, come compare notes with other Texans in our Insurance Claims community.
